content: The child was found to have elevated cadmium levels in his urine, measured in grams per liter. It was discovered that he had a habit of licking freshly polished white shoes, which were treated with a polish solution containing 275 micrograms of cadmium per 100 milliliters. Occasionally, he also consumed silver polish containing 185 micrograms of cadmium per 100 milliliters and ingested red paint from his crib, which contained 500 milligrams of cadmium per 100 grams. Buchet et al. analyzed chromosomes in lymphocytes from Swedish battery factory workers and Japanese Itai-Itai disease patients, comparing them to control groups from Sweden and Japan. They found no significant differences in chromosomal aberrations between cadmium-exposed individuals and their respective controls. However, the sample sizes in these studies were small. Shiraishi and colleagues cultured cadmium sulfide with human leukocyte cells and examined the chromosomes of leukocytes from seven Itai-Itai patients. They observed an increased incidence of chromosomal aberrations in these patients compared to controls. The rate of abnormalities in the Itai-Itai patients ranged from 14% to 64% of the 50 cells examined, which was significantly higher than the rates reported by Buchet et al. Bonnell studied 100 workers exposed to cadmium oxide fumes and 104 controls of similar age distribution in two British copper-cadmium alloy factories. Among the exposed workers, 19 individuals exhibited signs of emphysema, proteinuria, or both, compared to only three individuals in the control group. All 19 affected workers had been exposed to cadmium for more than five years, and 13 of them for over 15 years. Four additional workers required hospitalization due to shortness of breath. Kazantzis found significant differences in respiratory function test results between exposed and control groups, particularly in the time constant of the expiratory forced vital capacity curve. Buxton reported that workers exposed to cadmium for more than 10 years had significantly increased residual air volume and residual quotient (residual air as a percentage of total lung volume). Friberg and colleagues studied 110 cadmium-exposed workers and 22 controls, finding that kidney function declined with prolonged exposure. Urinary protein excretion increased with the duration of exposure, ranging from 100 mg/24 hours (50–170 mg) in workers exposed for less than five years to 955 mg/24 hours (370–1800 mg) in those exposed for 31 years or more. In the age group 50–59, there was a statistically insignificant increase in hypertension among exposed women. A significant increase in average haptoglobin and sedimentation rate was observed in the 40–49 age group, with a nonsignificant increase in the 18–29 age group. Serum iron levels were lower in the 50–59 age group. No significant differences in urinary findings were noted, except for one control case with high β2-microglobulin excretion, suggesting tubular dysfunction without glucose in the urine or bacterial infection. A 71-year-old exposed woman exhibited slight tubular dysfunction without increased β2-microglobulin excretion; she had been classified as a suspect case in 1969. Piscator et al. observed significant differences in blood and urine cadmium levels, noting that urinary cadmium increased with age, but blood cadmium did not. They also found a slight decrease in urinary zinc with prolonged exposure, except in cases where zinc levels were elevated due to antihypertensive drug use. Smokers had significantly higher blood cadmium levels than non-smokers. However, no differences were found in urinary cadmium excretion between cadmium-exposed smokers and non-smokers, although control smokers excreted more cadmium than control non-smokers. It was hypothesized that cadmium might have been deposited on cigarettes during work, vaporized during smoking, and subsequently inhaled. A significant correlation between blood and urine cadmium levels was found in non-smokers exposed for less than 10 years, but not in smokers. Kjellström and colleagues studied β2-microglobulin excretion in male and female workers from a battery factory previously studied by Friberg. The study included 240 exposed workers (both male and female) and 87 unexposed male controls. The exposed workers were employed in departments where materials for battery electrodes were produced (material plant) or where electrodes and batteries were assembled (assembly plant).
